chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Abdullah ibn Amir, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Al-Hasan ibn Al-Fadl, from Ghalib ibn Uthman, from Bashir al-Dahhan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

God Mighty and Majestic said: "Whichever servant I afflict with an affliction, and he conceals it from his visitors for three (days), I will replace his flesh with flesh better than his, and blood better than his, and skin better than his. So if I keep him alive, I keep him without sin, and if he dies, he dies unto My mercy."

key_terms.أَبْدَلَ: to replace, exchange, substitute — here referring to divine renewal of the body
key_terms.بَشَر: skin, human skin (outer layer of the body)
key_terms.بَلِيَّة: affliction, trial, calamity — a divinely-sent test
key_terms.رَحْمَة: mercy, compassion — a fundamental divine attribute
key_terms.عُوَّاد: visitors, those who come to visit the sick (from 'awada, to visit the ill)

ai.seo_question: What does God promise the believer who patiently conceals their illness from visitors according to Al-Kafi?
ai.summary: This is a hadith qudsi (divine saying) transmitted through Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him), in which God promises immense spiritual and physical renewal to the believer who, upon being tested with illness or hardship, bears it patiently without complaining to visitors for three days. The divine promise has two outcomes: if the patient recovers, God purifies him of sin; if he dies, he departs to God's mercy. This hadith reflects the Islamic understanding that patient endurance of affliction, particularly concealing one's suffering out of dignity and trust in God, is a virtue that merits extraordinary divine reward. The Shia tradition understood 'three days' as a threshold of meaningful patience rather than a strict legal limit.
